drug_class: Parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) analog / Bone-building agent
purpose: Abaloparatide is used to treat osteoporosis in women after menopause who are at high risk of breaking a bone. It helps make bones stronger and reduces the chance of fractures, especially in the spine and hip. Doctors may also prescribe it for men with osteoporosis at high risk for fractures.
how_it_works: Your body has a natural hormone that helps control how your bones are built and maintained. Abaloparatide works like that hormone by stimulating special cells in your bones called osteoblasts, which are the cells responsible for building new bone. This helps your body add new bone mass, making your bones thicker and stronger over time.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include dizziness, nausea, headache, and a fast heartbeat — especially shortly after your injection. You may also notice redness, pain, or bruising at the injection site. Some people feel lightheaded when standing up quickly, so take your time getting up after your injection.
warnings: This medication carries a boxed warning because it has caused bone tumors called osteosarcoma in animal studies, though this has not been confirmed in humans. It should not be used for more than 2 years in your lifetime. Tell your doctor if you have a history of bone cancer, Paget's disease of bone, unexplained high calcium levels, or have had radiation to your bones. Always sit or lie down for at least 30 minutes after your injection in case you feel dizzy or faint.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 80 micrograms injected under the skin (subcutaneously) in your abdomen once every day. It comes as a prefilled injection pen that you use yourself at home. Your doctor will show you exactly how to use it. Inject it at the same time each day, and rotate the spot on your belly slightly each time.
